issues.legal_issue: A final decision on an issue between the same parties in a proceeding binds them at a later stage of that proceeding, unless the issue concerns jurisdiction or conflicts with a statutory direction or prohibition.
material_facts: Earlier orders in the same proceedings between the parties permitted the principal’s existing power-of-attorney holder to appear only in that capacity, not as an advocate.
At a later stage, the opposing party again challenged the holder’s participation, including her examination of witnesses.
The earlier orders had been made by a competent court and had not been set aside or modified.
The Supreme Court found that the earlier orders did not conflict with a statutory prohibition or raise a jurisdictional issue.
issues.conclusion: The earlier orders operated as res judicata and barred reopening the issue of the holder’s capacity in the same proceedings. The High Court erred in deciding otherwise; its order was set aside and the trial court’s orders were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 reflects the general doctrine of res judicata. The doctrine applies at a later stage of the same proceeding as well as in subsequent proceedings: Y.B. Patil v. Y.L. Patil. Even an erroneous decision between the same parties binds them when made by a competent court: Gorie Gouri Naidu v. Thandrothu Bodemma. A binding decision cannot be disregarded as per incuriam on principles applicable to precedent: S. Nagaraj v. B.R. Vasudeva Murthy. The doctrine does not apply where the issue concerns jurisdiction or giving effect to the decision would conflict with a statutory direction or prohibition: Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy and Allahabad Development Authority v. Nasiruzzaman. The doctrine is founded on finality and public policy: Daryao v. State of U.P.; Lal Chand v. Radha Krishan. A precedent binds in similar cases, whereas res judicata binds the parties to the proceedings: Makhija Construction & Engineering (P) Ltd. v. Indore Development Authority.

rule.if: same_proceeding_stage and same_parties and same_issue_finally_decided_by_competent_court and not jurisdiction_or_statutory_conflict

predicates.same_proceeding_stage: The later dispute arose at a subsequent stage of the same proceeding in which the earlier decision was made.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later dispute were the same parties, or their privies, as those bound by the earlier decision.
predicates.same_issue_finally_decided_by_competent_: A competent court had finally decided the same issue between those parties.
predicates.jurisdiction_or_statutory_conflict: The issue concerns the court’s jurisdiction or giving effect to the earlier decision would conflict with a statutory direction or prohibition.

issues.definition: When the same parties raise at a later stage of the same proceeding an issue already finally decided by a competent court, and the issue involves no jurisdictional or statutory conflict, the earlier decision bars relitigation.

issues.legal_issue: An existing power-of-attorney holder is not disqualified from appearing solely in that capacity because the holder later becomes an enrolled advocate.
material_facts: The principal had appointed the holder as a power-of-attorney agent before she became an enrolled advocate.
The holder became enrolled as an advocate while the proceedings were pending.
Earlier orders permitted her to appear only as the principal’s power-of-attorney holder and not in her professional capacity as an advocate.
The holder sought to participate in the proceedings, including examining witnesses, as the agent rather than as counsel.
issues.conclusion: Section 32 of the Advocates Act, 1961 does not create a prohibition against permitting an existing power-of-attorney holder to appear as such merely because the holder later becomes an advocate. The earlier orders permitting that capacity remained binding in these proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32 of the Advocates Act, 1961 enables a court, authority, or person to permit a non-advocate to appear in a particular case; it does not create a corresponding prohibition against permitting an existing power-of-attorney holder to appear in that capacity after becoming enrolled as an advocate. Order III Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 concern appearances and acts by recognized agents. The court emphasized that the holder must act as the agent, not in her professional capacity as an advocate. The ruling also rested on the binding prior orders between the parties in the same proceedings.

rule.if: civil_proceeding and existing_power_of_attorney_holder and enrolled_after_appointment and court_permission_granted and acts_only_as_agent

predicates.civil_proceeding: The matter is a civil proceeding in which a party may appear through a recognized agent.
predicates.existing_power_of_attorney_holder: The person was already authorized to act for the principal under a power of attorney.
predicates.enrolled_after_appointment: The person became an enrolled advocate after being appointed as the principal’s power-of-attorney holder.
predicates.court_permission_granted: The court permitted the person to appear for the principal in the proceeding.
predicates.acts_only_as_agent: The person appears and acts only in the capacity of the principal’s agent, not in a professional capacity as an advocate.

issues.definition: When a court permits an existing agent who became an advocate after appointment to act only as the principal’s agent, that later enrollment alone does not bar the agent’s appearance.
